alarmAnalytics.body:
■ What this page is for
Alarm analytics turns a period of alarms into statistics. It helps find problems such as too many alarms, chattering alarms, or alarms that nobody handles, instead of looking at alarms one by one.

■ What is on the page
1. Filters: start and end time, area, level, rule and Top N. Click Query to apply changes.
2. KPI cards: alarm counts per operator per 10 minutes, hour and day, flood share, acknowledgement time, recovery time, long-standing alarms, shelving and suppression.
3. Charts: alarms per 10 minutes, alarms by level, priority distribution and a bad-actor ranking (Pareto chart: ranked from most to least). Click a chart or table row to inspect the matching alarm details.
4. Analysis tables: most frequent, chattering, transient, related/duplicate, flood and long-standing alarms.
5. Recommendations: suggested merges, threshold changes or delays, with current and suggested values.
6. Analysis thresholds: edit the definitions of flood, chattering, transient and long-standing alarms, then re-analyse.
7. Export: Excel or PDF.

■ How to use it
1. Choose the date range; narrow it by area, level or rule if needed.
2. Click Query and read the KPI cards to see whether alarm load is abnormal.
3. Review trends, Pareto and recommendations to find the rules that need work.
4. Export Excel or PDF when sharing the result.

■ Good to know
When the data volume is too large, the system analyses only a recent part and says so. Narrow the range for complete results. These statistics show patterns; they do not replace checking a specific alarm on site.
alarmAnalytics.summary: A health report for alarms: which alarms are most frequent, how fast they are acknowledged, and whether floods occur.
alarmAnalytics.title: Alarm analytics

alarmRules.body:
■ What this page is for
Alarm rules are the decision criteria for alarms. For example, temperature above 80 may be a warning and above 100 critical. Rules decide when an alarm fires and what message operators see.

■ What is on the page
1. Filters: tag name, alarm message and enabled state; batch enable, disable and delete.
2. Rule list: tag, type, threshold, level, trigger/recovery delay, recovery deadband, conditional suppression, message and actions.
3. Create/edit: choose the rule type (high, low, high-high, low-low, change, state and so on), then set threshold, level, delay, deadband, condition tag and message.
4. Cause and action: optional text explaining why it alarms and what the field should do, shown to operators.
5. Four-limit batch generation: fills high-high, high, low and low-low starting values from the tag range and creates only rules that do not exist yet.

■ How to use it
1. Click New rule and choose a tag.
2. Select the rule type and level, then enter the threshold; add delay and deadband if needed.
3. Write the alarm message, cause and action, then save.
4. Use Four-limit batch generation to add the four limit rules at once, checking the suggested values first.

■ Good to know
A trigger delay prevents a momentary spike from causing an alarm. A recovery deadband prevents alarms from toggling around the threshold. Conditional suppression only alarms while the condition tag is true, useful when monitoring is needed only while a machine is running.
alarmRules.summary: Tell the system what counts as an alarm, which level it is, and whether it needs a delay.
alarmRules.title: Alarm rules

alarms.body:
■ What this page is for
Alarms is where field alarms are handled. An alarm is a device asking for help. This page separates alarms that are still active, alarms that have recovered but are not acknowledged, and alarms that are temporarily shelved.

■ What is on the page
1. Three tabs: Live, Shelved, and History.
2. State filters: all active, unacknowledged, returned-unacknowledged, acknowledged, shelved, suppressed. The filter buttons support keyboard focus and Enter/Space selection.
3. Query fields: history supports a time range, level and keyword, plus priority-first or newest-first sorting.
4. Alarm table: state, level, message, value, start time, duration, end time and acknowledger. A First out marker identifies the earliest alarm in a flood.
5. Actions: acknowledge one alarm, add a note, shelve an alarm, batch acknowledge, or acknowledge visible. The Annunciator silence button only quiets the horn; it does not acknowledge alarms.
6. Processing record: open an alarm to see its occurrence, acknowledgement, notes and notification history.

■ How to use it
1. Choose a tab and state, for example Unacknowledged first.
2. Select the alarm and click Acknowledge; add a handling note if needed.
3. If work is not finished but the alarm should stop reminding, click Shelve and set a duration and reason. It clears automatically.
4. For history, set the start and end times and click Query.

■ Good to know
Annunciator silence does not acknowledge alarms and does not change the browser sound switch. Batch acknowledge only affects confirmable records on the current page. If the page says conditions changed, the table still shows the previous query until you click Query.
alarms.summary: The alarm workbench: see what is unacknowledged, what has recovered, and what is temporarily shelved.
alarms.title: Alarms

annunciators.body:
■ What this page is for
Annunciator controls field horns, buzzers or stack lights. When an alarm occurs, it can turn on output tags so operators notice problems without staring at a computer.

■ What is on the page
1. Panel list: name, area, enabled state, latch/follow mode, number of outputs and current state.
2. Actions: Silence, Unsilence, Test, Edit and Delete. Test only checks that the horn and light work.
3. Create/edit panel: name, area, silence minutes, browser sound and output tags. One panel can have several outputs.
4. State labels: Silenced means the sound is temporarily off; Idle means no output; Horn on means it is currently sounding.

■ How to use it
1. Click New panel and enter a name and area.
2. Add output tags and choose the digital outputs to switch on for alarms.
3. Set silence duration and browser sound, then save and enable.
4. During an alarm, click Silence to quiet the field temporarily and Unsilence when done.

■ Good to know
Silencing affects only the horn and light; it does not acknowledge the alarm. Browser alarm sound is a separate switch in the header. Output tags must be writable digital tags; verify addresses before enabling to avoid unintended operation.
annunciators.summary: Connect alarms to physical horns and stack lights so the shop floor can hear and see them.
annunciators.title: Annunciator

calcJobs.body:
■ What this page is for
Calculation jobs go beyond ordinary calculated tags. They can count pulses, integrate instantaneous flow into a total, split totals into time bands, and run custom logic in a C# Worker when advanced scripts are enabled.

■ What is on the page
1. Job list: name, type, version, input/cycle, current result, maintenance due, running state and actions.
2. Actions: create, edit, enable/disable, view snapshot, reset, acknowledge unknown command, maintenance complete, delete.
3. Parameters: name, type, area, cycle, input method, pulse weight, conversion factor, counter full scale, maximum increment, run threshold, maintenance threshold, bad-quality handling, cycle reset, time bands and unit.
4. Advanced script: readable/writable tags, input validity, output unit and script content, with compile and Preview (not dispatched). The script runs in a C# Worker (a background process for custom scripts).
5. Snapshots: time, reason, cycle and value before a reset for later checking.

■ How to use it
1. Click New calculation job and choose the type, for example pulse count or flow integration.
2. Enter the input tag, conversion factor, unit and cycle.
3. Add time bands when banded totals are needed; enable advanced scripts only for custom logic.
4. Save and enable. When maintenance is due, handle it and click Maintenance complete.

■ Good to know
Reset clears the accumulated value; check the snapshot and confirm that the field allows it. The C# Worker is disabled by default and requires server-side permission and isolation configuration. Preview never sends or writes real values.
calcJobs.summary: Handle more complex background work such as pulse counting, flow integration and advanced scripts.
calcJobs.title: Calculation jobs

calculations.body:
■ What this page is for
Calculated tags use existing tag values instead of installing new sensors. For example, output divided by time gives rate, and outlet temperature minus inlet temperature gives the difference.

■ What is on the page
1. List: calculated tag name, version, expression, run settings, input validity, current value/quality and time hints.
2. Actions: create, edit and delete, plus refresh calculation state.
3. Expression editor: reference input tags as #id and use arithmetic, comparison, logic and whitelisted built-in functions. Insert tag reference searches by name.
4. Run settings: enable/disable, calculation cycle, input validity, unit, storage mode and history deadband.
5. Validate and preview: run Validate and preview before saving to confirm the formula produces a result.

■ How to use it
1. Click New calculated tag and enter a name and description.
2. Insert the tags you need and write a formula such as #12 + #15.
3. Click Validate and preview and check the preview value.
4. Set the cycle and validity, then save and enable.

■ Good to know
If an input is older than its validity, the calculation is treated as invalid rather than reusing an old value. Only the system's numeric expression syntax is allowed; C#, JavaScript and other scripts are not accepted. Always preview before saving.
calculations.summary: Create new tags from existing values with a formula, such as efficiency, difference or average.
calculations.title: Calculated tags

console.body:
■ What this page is for
The runtime workbench combines several process screens into one operator window. Operators can watch multiple areas without switching pages, and the top strip shows the most severe alarm.

■ What is on the page
1. Top toolbar: choose a layout, switch monitor, see workstation state, choose the target region, open configuration, monitor-only switch, refresh, fullscreen and return to Overview.
2. Alarm banner: the most severe alarm, unacknowledged/active counts and returned-but-unacknowledged count. Only the first few alarms are listed when there are many.
3. Screen regions: the configured grid showing process screens, alarm lists, screen directories and so on.
4. Alarm list: level, state, start time, message and acknowledge button; authorised users can acknowledge here.
5. Update notice: appears when a newly published layout version is available; click Apply update to switch.

■ How to use it
1. Choose a layout; on multiple monitors, switch to the matching monitor.
2. Read the top alarm banner and handle the most severe alarm first.
3. Use Open into to choose a target region when needed.
4. Use Fullscreen for large displays and Back to return to Overview.

■ Good to know
Monitor-only mode disables control actions and is suitable for large displays. Control actions are also disabled in draft preview. After a layout update, click Apply update; the switch does not interrupt the current operation automatically.
console.summary: The operator runtime: several screens in one window, with the most important alarm at the top.
console.title: Runtime workbench

control.body:
■ What this page is for
Field control is the dispatch desk for control actions. Some actions need a second person to approve them, some equipment is locked out, and some processes run automatically step by step. All these rules are managed here.

■ What is on the page
1. Approval rules tab: pending recipe downloads and sequence runs, with Approve, Withdraw and Reject.
2. Locks tab: place a No operation or Maintenance lock on a device or tag to prevent mistakes, and remove it when done.
3. Control mode tab: shows whether a device is Local or Remote. Local means the field has taken over and the centre cannot send commands; switching back to Remote requires a reason.
4. Sequences tab: define sequences (automatic step-by-step processes) with write, wait, condition, branch, timeout and failure handling steps; run, view run records and flow charts, and abort.
5. Control policies tab: configure confirmation, dual approval, validity, limits, permit/interlock conditions and feedback conditions for writable tags.

■ How to use it
1. Check Approval rules and approve a request after verifying its content.
2. Place a Maintenance lock before servicing equipment and remove it afterwards.
3. Switch a device to Local when the centre must not operate it; switch back to Remote with a reason when finished.
4. Create a sequence and add steps, test it, then run it.

■ Good to know
Locks, mode switching and sequence runs are control actions requiring permission. A reason is mandatory when returning to Remote for later auditing. Run records keep the result of every step; check them and the flow chart when troubleshooting.
control.summary: Manage approvals, equipment locks, local/remote mode, sequences and control policies in one place.
control.title: Field control

devices.body:
■ What this page is for
Device configuration is the collection system address book. It records the protocol, address, collection cycle and area for every device.

■ What is on the page
1. Filters: device name, address, area, protocol and enabled state; Show all devices clears the scope.
2. Single-device actions: add, edit, copy, delete, test connection, collection diagnostics, browse variables (OPC UA) and change collection location.
3. Batch actions: enable, disable and delete in bulk, plus OPC UA certificates.
4. Device form: the basic section holds name, area, protocol and connection parameters; the advanced section holds byte order, collection cycle and timeout.
5. Gateway devices: a device collected by a gateway shows Gateway #number; entering from the gateway page limits the list to that gateway.

■ How to use it
1. Click New device, choose the protocol and enter the address and port/serial settings.
2. Save, then click Test connection to confirm a raw value can be read.
3. When the connection works, add tags or use Browse variables for OPC UA.
4. Disable a device instead of deleting it when possible, to preserve tag links.

■ Good to know
Saving does not prove the connection works; always test. New devices start disabled and are registered at the centre. If a gateway collects the device, assign it to that gateway. Failed tests keep the original error and show troubleshooting advice; do not bypass security checks to make a test pass.
devices.summary: Register each PLC, instrument or gateway and tell the system how to connect to it.
devices.title: Device configuration

externalApi.body:
■ What this page is for
The external API lets other systems, such as MES, report platforms or dashboards, read data from this system. Here you can see whether REST, TCP, OPC UA and OpenAPI are enabled and create or manage API keys.

■ What is on the page
1. Interface status: whether four interfaces are enabled: REST (the common data interface for web pages and programs), TCP (a raw network connection), OPC UA (a common industrial device protocol) and OpenAPI (a published interface description).
2. Key list: name, prefix, scopes, areas, per-minute limit, enabled state and actions.
3. New key: enter a note and configure scopes and areas after creation.
4. Plain key: shown once after creation; copy it immediately. It cannot be viewed again after closing.
5. Revoke: revocation cannot be undone and requires confirmation.

■ How to use it
1. Confirm the interface you need is enabled.
2. Click New key, enter a note and copy the key immediately.
3. Grant the minimum scopes and areas and set a per-minute limit.
4. Revoke a key when it is no longer used or may have leaked.

■ Good to know
An API key is like a password and is shown only once. Do not grant more access than the external system needs, and distinguish read-only from write access. Revocation is permanent; confirm the external system has switched to a new key first.
externalApi.summary: Manage the interfaces and keys external systems use, including what they can access and how fast.
externalApi.title: External API

gateways.body:
■ What this page is for
A collection gateway is a small local post office near the equipment. It collects PLC data and sends it to the central server, so the centre does not need to connect to every device directly.

■ What is on the page
1. Gateway list: name, process version, centre connection state, configuration state, device count, last heartbeat, pending transfer and actions.
2. Single-gateway actions: details, edit name, disable/enable, rotate key, release session.
3. Create gateway: generates a one-time key shown only once; it can be copied or downloaded.
4. Gateway details: lease expiry, process version, configuration confirmation, remote engineering support, pending backlog, centre configuration summary and assigned devices.
5. Assigned devices: name, protocol, tag count, state and collection hints; change collection location or open device configuration.

■ How to use it
1. Click New gateway, save it and keep the generated key safe.
2. Configure the centre address and key on the gateway so it can connect.
3. Check Configuration confirmed and the heartbeat on the details page, then assign devices.
4. Before replacing or reinstalling a gateway, stop the old one, then rotate the key or release the session.

■ Good to know
The key is shown only once and cannot be recovered; rotate it if lost. Release a session only after confirming that the old gateway process and field I/O have stopped, otherwise two gateways may collect duplicate data.
gateways.summary: When devices are remote or hard to reach, a gateway collects data nearby and forwards it to the centre.
gateways.title: Collection gateways

hmiLibrary.body:
■ What this page is for
Symbols & templates is the parts library for process screens. Pumps, valves, meters, trend widgets and reusable panel templates are managed and previewed here.

■ What is on the page
1. Import/export: import SVG symbols or a library JSON, and export the library.
2. Built-in symbols: preview built-in widgets in preview, stopped, running, alarm and unknown states.
3. User library: imported symbols and templates with key, name, category, placeholders, reference state and actions.
4. Template editing: change template name, category and placeholders; placeholders are replaced by tag bindings when the template is instantiated.
5. Refresh and delete: reload the list and delete unused custom symbols or templates.

■ How to use it
1. Browse the built-in symbols first.
2. Import an SVG or library JSON when you need new symbols.
3. To reuse a group of widgets, save it as a template in the screen designer and edit it here.
4. Check the referenced state before deleting anything.

■ Good to know
Deleting a symbol used by a screen or template can break its display. Changes to a template update all instances; to change only one screen, copy the template or edit the instance directly.
hmiLibrary.summary: Manage the symbols, icons and panel templates available in process screens.
hmiLibrary.title: Symbols & templates

layouts.body:
■ What this page is for
Workbench configuration arranges runtime layouts: how many monitors, how each screen is divided, and which screen goes in each region. After configuration and publishing, operators can use it in the runtime workbench.

■ What is on the page
1. Local workstation: register this computer as a workstation, choose its default layout and whether control is allowed.
2. Layout list: search and filter by publication and workstation usage; shows published version, draft changes, runtime name and usage.
3. New layout: quick creation, or advanced mode with grid, monitors and regions.
4. Layout editor: monitor count, grid (rows and columns dividing the screen), region position, row/column spans, region type (screen, alarms, screen directory and so on), published screen binding, title and properties.
5. Save and publish: Save draft first, then Publish after validation passes; only then can a workstation open it.
6. Preview: preview the runtime appearance from the configuration page.
7. Local draft: edits are staged in this browser; if they are not saved to the server, the page offers restore or discard.

■ How to use it
1. Register this workstation if this computer will run the workbench.
2. Create a layout, add monitors and set the grid.
3. Choose a screen or type for each region and adjust position and size.
4. Save draft, resolve validation issues and publish.
5. Open the layout in the runtime workbench to check it.

■ Good to know
Saving a draft is not publishing; unpublished layouts cannot run on a workstation. After changes, publish again so the runtime sees the new version. Check for regions that would move outside the grid before shrinking or deleting a monitor.
layouts.summary: Arrange screens and alarm strips into a workbench so operators can see a whole line at a glance.
layouts.title: Workbench configuration

license.body:
■ What this page is for
The software licence confirms that this system is properly licensed, how long it is valid, and how many devices and tags it allows. When the licence expires or limits are exceeded, some features may be restricted.

■ What is on the page
1. Licence information: licence number, customer, expiry, days remaining, device limit and tag limit.
2. Feature list: basic features and other licensed features.
3. Machine code: the current server machine code, with Copy to send to the vendor.
4. Activation code: paste a code beginning with SCADA1. and click Activate.
5. Status notices: trial expiry or approaching expiry warnings.

■ How to use it
1. Copy the machine code and send it to the vendor to request a licence.
2. When the activation code arrives, paste it and click Activate.
3. After activation, verify expiry, limits and the feature list.

■ Good to know
Only administrators with user-management permission can activate the software. The machine code is bound to the server, so a replacement machine needs a new licence. Keep the activation code confidential.
license.summary: Check licence state, machine code, expiry and device/tag limits, and enter an activation code.
license.title: Software license

measurementReports.body:
■ What this page is for
Tag statistics is for quick historical queries, such as the average temperature yesterday. It is suitable for checking data, not for formal report archiving.

■ What is on the page
1. Report type: daily or monthly.
2. Time range: start and end dates for daily reports, start and end months for monthly reports.
3. Tag selection: search and tick the tags to include; the selected count is shown.
4. Generate report: shows time, tag, average, minimum, maximum and sample count.
5. Export Excel: saves the current result as a spreadsheet.
6. Status hints: warns when no tags are available or when conditions changed without regenerating.

■ How to use it
1. Choose daily or monthly.
2. Select the time range and tags.
3. Click Generate report and wait for the result.
4. Click Export Excel when sharing the data.

■ Good to know
This creates a temporary query, not an archived report. For formal reports with signatures or email delivery, use Business reports. Larger ranges and many tags take longer, so start with a small selection.
measurementReports.summary: Temporarily query the average, minimum and maximum of tags over a period and export to Excel.
measurementReports.title: Tag statistics

notifications.body:
■ What this page is for
Alarm notifications deliver alarms outside the screen. Email, SMS or webhook calls can reach people who are not at the computer.

■ What is on the page
1. Notification routes: name, area, minimum level, shift, channel, trigger conditions, unacknowledged escalation minutes, alarm/recovery events, recipients and enabled state.
2. Notification channels: SMTP email, SMS or webhook (a network address that lets one program notify another) with address and credentials. Credentials are encrypted and shown as ***. Test verifies the channel.
3. Shifts: times and weekday rules deciding when notifications are sent.
4. Delivery failures: action, count, last error and failure time; mark as known, or mark all as known.
5. Refresh: reload configuration and failures.

■ How to use it
1. Create and test a channel on the Notification channels tab.
2. Create a route, choose the channel, area, level and recipients, and set trigger and escalation times.
3. Configure shifts when delivery should follow a timetable.
4. Investigate delivery failures and mark them as known after handling.

■ Good to know
Saved credentials are never shown; leave the field blank to keep the current value. A route needs a channel first. Escalation means the alarm is sent to the next level after being unacknowledged for the set time. Testing a channel sends a real message.
notifications.summary: Send alarms by email, SMS or webhook and decide who receives them and when.
notifications.title: Alarm notifications

objectTemplateEditor.body:
■ What this page is for
The object template editor is the editing bench for templates. Define which tags and alarms a typical device needs and what its panel looks like. Once published, other pages can use the template to generate device objects in batches.

■ What is on the page
1. Top state: template name, unsaved/saved, current draft revision and latest published version.
2. Tag definitions: add template tags with logical key, name, area, offset, type, unit, multiplier, offset value, limits, writable, archive mode and description. Addresses are instance base address plus relative offset.
3. Alarm definitions: bind alarms to template tags with logical key, threshold, level, delay, recovery deadband, message and enabled state.
4. Panel template: widgets used when the template generates a device panel.
5. Publication history: published version, time, publisher and content; published versions are read-only snapshots.
6. Actions: validate, save and publish a new version.

■ How to use it
1. Fill in tag definitions; offsets must follow the device address pattern.
2. Add alarm definitions and bind the matching template tags.
3. Click Validate template and fix the reported issues.
4. Save the draft, then publish a new version when ready.

■ Good to know
Published versions cannot be edited directly; edit the draft and publish again to create a new version. Logical keys map the model internally, so avoid renaming them after publishing. Offsets start from the instance base address; a wrong offset makes batch-generated devices read the wrong address.
objectTemplateEditor.summary: Edit tags, alarms and panels in a device template, then validate, save and publish a new version.
objectTemplateEditor.title: Object template editor

objectTemplates.body:
■ What this page is for
Device objects & templates is for many identical devices. Ten identical pumps may have the same tag layout, alarm rules and panel structure, differing only in base address. Create one template and generate ten objects.

■ What is on the page
1. Template list: device template, published version, draft state, object instance count and actions.
2. Template actions: create, edit, batch generate and delete.
3. Object instances: object name, collection device, source template, base address, version and actions.
4. Batch generation: template version, name prefix, starting number, object count, starting base address and address spacing; the preview shows how many tags, alarms and widgets will be created.
5. Upgrade selected objects: when a new template version is published, upgrade existing objects; preview three-way differences and choose conflict handling first.
6. Unlink: stop an object from following template versions.

■ How to use it
1. Build and publish a template in the template editor.
2. Click Batch generate objects and set the count and base address.
3. Check the preview for address overflow, then click Confirm generation.
4. For template upgrades, select objects, click Upgrade selected objects and resolve conflicts based on the preview.

■ Good to know
Batch generation creates real tags, alarms and device panel drafts, so check base addresses and spacing against device limits before running. Keep field configuration and Adopt template have different effects on existing configuration; review differences before confirming.
objectTemplates.summary: Use template plus batch generation to create tags, alarms and panels for many similar devices at once.
objectTemplates.title: Device objects & templates

oee.body:
■ What this page is for
OEE means Overall Equipment Effectiveness. Think of it as three questions multiplied together: how much of the planned time the line actually ran (Availability A), how fast it ran while running (Performance P), and how much of the output was good (Quality Q).

■ What is on the page
1. Filters: time range, area, line, product and shift. Click Query; if conditions changed without querying, the page warns that the previous result is still shown.
2. Core metrics: OEE, Availability A, Performance P and Quality Q, plus targets for comparison.
3. Supporting metrics: good count, scrap rate, run/planned hours, failure count and output/target.
4. Charts: OEE trend, downtime Pareto (which downtime reason takes the most time), by shift, by product and by day.
5. Drill-down: View day narrows to a day; Production events lets you record downtime or correct output.
6. Export: Excel and PDF.

■ How to use it
1. Choose a line and time range, then click Query.
2. Check which of OEE, A, P and Q is the weakest: low A usually means downtime, low P usually means slow running, low Q usually means scrap.
3. Use the downtime Pareto to find the largest reason.
4. Use Production events to record or correct the underlying data.

■ Good to know
For long ranges, early parts may use pre-aggregated data and detail starts from a recent window. OEE depends on complete line, shift, downtime-reason and output data; inaccurate input gives inaccurate results.
oee.summary: Use OEE to measure how much of the planned time ran, how fast it ran, and how much good product came out.
oee.title: OEE production

oeeConfig.body:
■ What this page is for
OEE configuration is the base dictionary for OEE statistics. The system needs to know the lines, products, shift divisions and downtime reasons before it can calculate OEE correctly.

■ What is on the page
1. Lines tab: add, edit and delete lines with name, area, ideal cycle time and enabled state.
2. Products tab: maintain product codes and related information.
3. Shifts tab: shift names with start and end minutes, which may cross midnight.
4. Downtime reasons tab: reason name, category and whether it is planned downtime.
5. OEE targets tab: target OEE, availability, performance and quality; performance is capped at 100%.
6. Production events link: opens the page for daily downtime recording and output corrections.

■ How to use it
1. Create lines first, then products and shifts.
2. Configure downtime reasons and distinguish planned downtime from faults or material shortages.
3. Set OEE targets and use OEE production for queries.
4. Do not record daily downtime here; use Production events.

■ Good to know
Lines, shifts and reasons are referenced by history, so check for active records before deleting them. Production events are daily operations; OEE configuration is master data. Keep the two separate.
oeeConfig.summary: Create lines, products, shifts, downtime reasons and OEE targets before the statistics can work.
oeeConfig.title: OEE configuration

ops.body:
■ What this page is for
Operations & HA keeps the system available. If the primary server fails, a standby can take over. This page shows primary/standby state, manual switchover, configuration and history replication, and backup/restore drills.

■ What is on the page
1. Primary/standby state: current node, term, peer node, last heartbeat, quorum (servers voting on who takes over) and lease (a temporary permission token).
2. Switch actions: Switch to standby or Take over on this node. Confirm the peer state before acting.
3. Automatic switching: enable or disable and see whether quorum is available.
4. Replication: configuration replication (copying configuration to the other server), applied history rows and lag.
5. Events: time, type, content, term and operator for switchovers and replication events.
6. Backup and restore drill: configure an off-site target, click Back up and drill now, and inspect packages, drill result and duration.
7. Monitoring: Prometheus scrape address.

■ How to use it
1. Check primary/standby state and heartbeat first.
2. Before maintaining the primary, confirm the standby is healthy and switch over.
3. Watch replication lag; investigate the network or load when it grows.
4. Run backup and restore drills regularly to prove backups are usable.

■ Good to know
Switchover is a high-availability action; confirm the peer state and field impact first so two nodes do not serve at once. When quorum is unavailable, automatic switching may be disabled and must be handled manually. Drills actually restore data, so schedule them in a maintenance window.
ops.summary: Check primary/standby servers, switch over, inspect replication and run backup drills.
ops.title: Operations & HA

overview.body:
■ What this page is for
The Overview is the plant dashboard. It brings together whether devices are online, whether alarms are active, and whether the system is healthy. It is the fastest place to look when you start a shift or begin an inspection round.

■ What is on the page
1. Top status bar: shows when the data was last updated, with a Refresh button. A stale-data warning means the latest data could not be read.
2. Summary cards: online devices, unacknowledged alarms, returned but unacknowledged alarms, and alarm floods (too many alarms in a short time). Clicking a card opens the matching alarm list.
3. Active alarms: level, message, trigger value, start time and acknowledgement state. Trend opens the history curve for that tag.
4. Device communication: online/offline state, last collection time, cycle and error for each device. Tick Only abnormal to find problem devices quickly.
5. Maintenance information at the bottom: channel backlog, history storage, uptime, and shortcuts to common pages.

■ How to use it
1. Check the summary cards first; handle red or large numbers first.
2. Open the alarm card or View all to acknowledge alarms on the Alarms page.
3. If a device is offline, click its name to open Realtime and inspect the collection error.
4. Click Refresh when you need current data; there is no need to switch pages.

■ Good to know
Alarm counts on the cards cover only the data loaded on this page, not necessarily the whole plant. Use the Alarms page for accurate query results.
overview.summary: A dashboard for the whole plant. Start here at shift handover or during rounds to see what is healthy and what needs attention.
overview.title: Overview

productionEvents.body:
■ What this page is for
Production events is the shop-floor production ledger. How long a machine stopped, why it stopped, and how much good or scrap product was made are recorded and corrected here. OEE statistics use this data directly.

■ What is on the page
1. Filters: line, start and end time, and confirmation state. Click Query.
2. Downtime event table: start/end time, duration in minutes, reason, confirmation state and source. An unfinished event shows as ongoing.
3. Confirmation: mark an event as confirmed and select product details where needed.
4. Output correction: enter good, defective and scrap quantities to correct previously counted output.
5. Link back to OEE production for comparison.

■ How to use it
1. Select a line and time range, then click Query.
2. When downtime ends, complete the reason and adjust the end time if necessary.
3. Click Confirm when the event is handled; use Output correction when quantities are wrong.
4. Return to OEE and query again to see the updated result.

■ Good to know
Confirming events and correcting output changes OEE statistics, so enter real values. The table shows at most 2000 records; narrow the range or filter by line when it is capped. Control permission for the line area is required; otherwise the page is read-only.
productionEvents.summary: Record downtime, classify reasons, confirm events and correct output for daily production.
productionEvents.title: Production events

project.body:
■ What this page is for
Project management handles the whole configuration, not just one tag or screen. Take a snapshot before major changes, compare versions, roll back, or export a project package to import elsewhere.

■ What is on the page
1. Export project: exports a package according to your permissions and shows its name, export time, size and partial-export notice.
2. Snapshots: enter a description and take a snapshot; the list shows revision, type, description, creation time, content and actions.
3. Compare: compare two versions and see the difference count.
4. Snapshot actions: roll back to this version or download.
5. Import and publish: choose a package, set the default conflict handling (skip, overwrite, import with new name), preview differences, then publish the import.

■ How to use it
1. Take a snapshot before major changes with a clear description such as pre-commissioning baseline.
2. After changes, take another snapshot and compare the two.
3. To restore, choose Roll back to this version and confirm.
4. To move systems, export the project and import it at the target.

■ Good to know
Rollback overwrites current configuration; take a snapshot or export first. Always preview import differences; conflict handling changes existing configuration. A permission-limited export may not contain everything.
project.summary: Back up, compare and roll back the whole configuration, or import it into another system.
project.title: Project management

realtime.body:
■ What this page is for
Realtime lists the values collected from field devices, such as temperature, pressure and production count. You can see what each tag is reading right now, and send a new setpoint to tags you are allowed to write.

■ What is on the page
1. Filter bar: filter by device, tag name or quality, or choose abnormal only / normal only. Click Query after changing filters.
2. Pause: Pause refresh freezes the current readings so you can inspect them; Continue refresh resumes automatic updates.
3. Tag table: device, tag name, value, quality, active alarms, sample time and description. Abnormal data is highlighted.
4. Actions: View trend, or Write for writable tags you are allowed to control.
5. Write dialog: shows the current value and range. Enter the target value and confirm. The system checks range, interlocks (conditions that limit each other), locks and control ownership, then writes and reads back.

■ How to use it
1. Choose a device or type a tag name, then click Query.
2. Find the tag and check its value, quality and sample time.
3. Click View trend to see how the value changed over time.
4. Click Write to change a setpoint, confirm the target, and check the read-back value afterwards.

■ Good to know
Writing is a control action and is limited by permissions, device mode and interlocks. Viewers can only read. If the mobile client is not allowed to control, writing is blocked there too. If a message says the original command number was kept, check the command receipt instead of submitting again.
realtime.summary: See the current value of every tag like reading a thermometer, and safely write setpoints when needed.
realtime.title: Realtime

recipes.body:
■ What this page is for
A recipe is like a cooking recipe: when a machine makes a different product, it needs different temperatures, pressures and times. Recipe management stores these parameter sets as versions and can send the whole batch to the device.

■ What is on the page
1. Recipe list: search by name, description or parameter, and filter by template. Shows parameter count, last change and actions.
2. Actions: create, upload from the field as a new recipe, edit, copy, view versions, compare with the field, download, upload and delete.
3. Download: runs a pre-check on range and type. If any parameter fails, nothing is downloaded. Recipes requiring review go through single or whole-batch dual approval.
4. Version history: each save creates a new version; compare two versions or compare with current field values.
5. Download records: recent submissions, status, read-back and execution. Failed records can be retried.
6. Template management: recipe templates, parameter ranges and review requirements.

■ How to use it
1. Choose a product or template and find the recipe.
2. Click Download; the system pre-checks the parameters.
3. Confirm the download and wait for read-back to verify the device reached the targets.
4. To change parameters, edit and save a new version, then download again.

■ Good to know
Downloading is a control action and needs control permission for the area. Recipes requiring dual approval must be approved by another authorised person. If the pre-check fails, no partial batch is sent; fix the recipe first.
recipes.summary: Package a set of process parameters as a recipe and send the whole batch to devices when needed.
recipes.title: Recipe management

reportCenter.body:
■ What this page is for
Business reports are formal production reports such as energy daily or assembly line production daily. Templates can generate files on a schedule or on demand, archive them, verify file integrity, and go through review and signing.

■ What is on the page
1. Templates and generation tab: maintain templates with period, area, shift start, scheduled generation, email channel, recipients and columns; generate the previous period, edit, copy, delete and view history.
2. Generated archives tab: filter by template, inspect period, template version, file state and signature state; preview, download, verify and sign.
3. Template editor: configure columns (tag, calculation job, output name, aggregation, decimals, unit) and add batches of tag columns, alarm KPI presets and OEE KPI presets.
4. Signing and approval: verify SHA256 and digital signatures, inspect review/approval records, and sign or reject step by step.
5. Refresh: re-read templates or archives.

■ How to use it
1. Create a template on the Templates and generation tab and configure its period and columns.
2. Click Generate previous period, or wait for the schedule.
3. On Generated archives, preview and download, then click Verify / sign when needed.
4. Complete review and approval; signing requires re-entering your own password.

■ Good to know
SHA256 and digital signatures prove a file has not been changed. Do not use a file that fails verification. Signing and approval require permissions, and the approver must not be the same person as the reviewer.
reportCenter.summary: Generate formal reports from templates, archive and download them, verify signatures and run review/sign-off.
reportCenter.title: Business reports

screenDesigner.body:
■ What this page is for
The screen designer builds process screens: drag pumps, valves, meters and other widgets (small parts on the screen) from the palette, arrange them, and bind tags so they show real data at runtime.

■ What is on the page
1. Left panel, components and layers: search widgets, drag or click to add, view layers, lock, hide and reorder.
2. Canvas: zoom, fit, locate the selection, grid snapping, alignment and grouping.
3. Right properties: position, size, style, text size, tag bindings, state mappings and actions.
4. Top toolbar: undo, redo, validate, preview, version history, save draft and publish.
5. Shortcuts: Shift multi-select, arrow-key nudge, Ctrl+C/V copy and paste, Ctrl+Z undo, Delete, Ctrl+A select all, Esc deselect.
6. Validation results: list issues such as tag bindings and navigation targets; click an item to locate the widget.

■ How to use it
1. Add widgets from the palette and drag them into place.
2. Bind tags in the properties panel and set units and number formats.
3. Configure state colours and click actions where needed.
4. Click Validate, fix issues, save the draft and publish.

■ Good to know
Publishing saves current changes first and checks tag bindings and navigation targets. Saving a draft does not update the field runtime. Do not configure write actions on tags that are not writable; the runtime will reject them.
screenDesigner.summary: Place widgets, bind tags and build equipment process screens like assembling blocks.
screenDesigner.title: Screen designer

screenRun.body:
■ What this page is for
Screen runtime opens a single published screen on a selected monitor. It is useful on multi-monitor industrial PCs, with one screen showing the overview and another showing equipment.

■ What is on the page
1. Back to screens: returns to the process screen list.
2. Select monitor: lists monitors the browser can see and marks the primary one.
3. Open in new window: opens the screen after confirmation.
4. Notice: if the browser does not support window management, a normal new window is used and must be moved manually.

■ How to use it
1. Click Run in the process screen list to reach this page.
2. Choose the target monitor.
3. Click Open; the window opens on that monitor.
4. Click Back to screens when finished.

■ Good to know
Only published screens can run. If the browser does not allow moving windows, no error appears; just drag the new window manually. Data and permissions still use the current login.
screenRun.summary: Choose a monitor and open a published process screen in a new window.
screenRun.title: Screen runtime

screens.body:
■ What this page is for
Process screens are the equipment dashboards operators use, usually with device drawings, live values, state lights and alarms. This page manages all screens, both published and draft.

■ What is on the page
1. Filters: search by screen name or modifier, filter by publication state, and sort by last modified or name.
2. Screen cards: name, draft/published revision, unpublished changes and the number of runtime layouts that use it.
3. Actions: preview, run, edit, copy and delete.
4. New screen: create a new screen or start from an existing one. Drafts are visible to administrators only; the field can run a screen only after publication.
5. Refresh: reload the screen list.

■ How to use it
1. Check whether the screen is published; drafts do not appear in the field runtime.
2. Click Preview to check it, or Run to open it in a new window.
3. Click Edit to open the screen designer.
4. Validate, save the draft and publish when done.

■ Good to know
Saving a draft is not publishing. After editing a published screen, publish again for the runtime to update. Before deleting, check whether a workbench layout still references the screen.
screens.summary: Manage the screens operators see: preview, run, edit, copy and publish them.
screens.title: Process screens

system.body:
■ What this page is for
System administration is the administrator back office: create accounts, assign area permissions, reset passwords, see who changed what, and check service health and history storage.

■ What is on the page
1. User management: create, edit name and display name, set role, enable/disable, area authorisation, reset password and delete.
2. Audit log: choose a time range and query by user, action or result; shows time, operator, action, tag, old/new value, change details, diff and result.
3. Areas and roles: manage areas and roles; custom roles can be limited to an area.
4. System status: runtime state, uptime, online devices, collected tags, bus backlog, disk space and history volume.
5. History capacity: raw history, aggregate history (long periods combined into averages, maxima and so on), database temporary log files (WAL/SHM), staging files, average daily growth, days to the warning threshold, retention and query limits.
6. Device status table: online/offline, last poll, cycle, tag count, reconnect count, communication failures and latest error.

■ How to use it
1. Create new users, choose a role and authorise areas.
2. Use the audit log when investigating a change.
3. Check system status and disk space regularly.
4. Notify the user after resetting a password or disabling an account.

■ Good to know
The administrator role applies to all areas; custom roles may cover one area. Check for active sessions before deleting a user. Retention and disk warning thresholds affect cleanup, so evaluate capacity before changing them.
system.summary: Manage users, inspect audit logs and check runtime health and history storage.
system.title: System administration

tags.body:
■ What this page is for
A tag is the smallest unit the collection system knows, such as Boiler 1 temperature or Line A01 output. Tag configuration tells the system where the value lives, what it is called, what type it is, and whether to store history.

■ What is on the page
1. Filters: search by device, name or description, or click Clear filters. Click Query after changing conditions.
2. Single-tag work: add, edit, copy and delete tags; configure alarm rules or calculation definitions.
3. Batch work: batch create, batch archive, batch delete, and import/export Excel.
4. Fields: device, name, description, area, type, address, scale/offset, unit, writable, storage mode, deadband and limits.
5. Tools: byte-order/address preview (byte order is how a number's high and low bytes are arranged in memory) and collection diagnostics to verify that addresses and reads are correct.

■ How to use it
1. Select a device and click Query to see existing tags.
2. When adding a tag, fill in name, type and address; the address area switches with the protocol.
3. For many similar tags, use Batch create and check names and addresses in the preview before creating.
4. After saving, use Read preview or Collection diagnostics to verify the value.

■ Good to know
Start address and quantity must match the device manual. S7 addresses start at byte 0, and digital tags also need a bit offset. Input area I is usually read-only. A wrong configuration will not damage the device, but it will read nothing or the wrong value.
tags.summary: A tag is one data point on a device. Here you define its name, address, type and storage.
tags.title: Tag configuration

traceability.body:
■ What this page is for
Traceability answers who made this product, when, and whether it passed inspection. Each product has a serial number (SN), and collected inspection data is stored under that SN.

■ What is on the page
1. Trace query: enter an SN, choose a collection job, inspection result and time range, then click Query. Expand a record to see all fields and units.
2. Scan binding: binds a scanned SN to the current collection job, showing pending SN, scan state, expiry and PLC reply.
3. Job configuration: create or edit scan jobs with device, SN source (web scan or PLC), SN format, register addresses, validity, TCP/serial settings and collection fields.
4. Inspection result mapping: optionally set pass and fail values so the page shows both the inspection result and the PLC reply. Without mapping it performs generic collection only.

■ How to use it
1. Enter an SN on the trace query and click Query.
2. Expand a record to inspect fields, values and units.
3. To collect a new product, bind its SN on the scan tab, then trigger inspection.
4. Create and enable a job on the configuration tab before first use.

■ Good to know
Stored, awaiting reply means the data is saved but the PLC handshake has not replied yet; it is not a failed inspection. A collection attempt without an SN records only the failure and does not create a product record. Jobs are disabled by default and must be enabled manually.
traceability.summary: Enter a product SN to find when, where and with what result it was produced.
traceability.title: Production traceability

trends.body:
■ What this page is for
Trends draws historical tag values as line charts, like a temperature record. It is the most direct way to compare time ranges and see whether something was abnormal before or after an event.

■ What is on the page
1. Tag selection: up to 50 tags at once. The number selected is shown, and Clear lets you start over.
2. Time range: use a preset or enter start and end times. If you change the conditions, click Query again to update.
3. Auto refresh: re-reads the data on a timer, useful when watching a live process.
4. Chart panels: tags with the same unit share a panel; different units are separated so temperature and pressure are not mixed on one axis.
5. Export CSV: saves the current result as a spreadsheet for Excel.
6. Resolution notice: large ranges may be downsampled, so digital transitions can be incomplete. Narrow the range to inspect raw changes.

■ How to use it
1. Select tags, then a time range.
2. Click Query and wait for the chart.
3. Hover over the curve to read a value at a point in time; select related tags to compare them.
4. Click Export CSV when you need the data elsewhere.

■ Good to know
Trends shows archived history, not the current instant. Use Realtime for current values. Larger ranges are more likely to be downsampled and lose detail.
trends.summary: Turn history into curves so you can see when a value changed and what it changed to.
trends.title: Trends
